prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The study used a randomized controlled trial design with 26 stroke patients split into two groups: one receiving real stimulation and the other receiving a fake version alongside standard therapy.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers applied electrical stimulation to the side of the cerebellum opposite to the side of the brain injury.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Participants performed simple walking or standing tasks alone and while counting backward to measure how much their performance dropped when doing two things at once.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The group receiving real stimulation showed a significant drop in the extra body movement cost when walking while doing a mental task.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The real stimulation group also improved their walking speed rhythm and the time spent with both feet on the ground during dual tasks.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Both groups showed better standing balance and walking ability, but the real stimulation group specifically reduced the extra cost of doing tasks together.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study found that the real stimulation group showed changes in brain wave activity and better connection between brain regions while walking and thinking.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Higher brain wave activity in the front of the brain was linked to better walking rhythm during dual tasks.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors suggest this stimulation technique could be a helpful addition to standard stroke recovery treatments.
facts.subject: humans
